paragraphs.text: The barrel is an ingenious and sophisticated piece of engineering. Constructed without nails or glue, it is a watertight container that is extremely tough. Moreover, its rounded shape means that when on its side, less than a square inch of surface area touches the ground, making it easy to roll — a barrel holding up to one hundred gallons can be moved with one hand. The barrel is one of the world's greatest transport inventions, with a design so successful that barrels today are little different from those constructed by the Bronze Age* craftsmen thought to have invented the device. The barrel has another remarkable feature: it can change the flavour of the food and drinks stored inside it. For some food producers, oak has become a powerful aid to creativity, generating an astonishing range of flavours depending on the climate in which the forest has grown, the grain of the tree, or the way the wood is seasoned.

Constructing a barrel is not easy. The job of the cooper (barrel maker) is to bind a series of staves** together with iron hoops. Getting the staves into the right shape is the first task. Each needs to narrow at both ends. It must have exactly the right curve and the edges must be cut at exactly the right angle so they fit snugly next to their neighbours. Flames or steam are used to bend the staves, to create the barrel's rounded surface. Then, the cooper hollows out the inside of the stave, and gives it a rounded shape on the outside, shaving off thin slices of wood until it is just right. Once all the staves have been made, they need to be assembled — another extremely difficult job. The staves are pulled together so a temporary hoop can be placed around them. The barrel is then left to cool and dry. Grooves are cut into the ends of each stave and the ‘head’ (the circular piece at each end of the barrel) is given sloping edges and hammered in place. Permanent hoops are then bound on to the barrel, which should be watertight.

Acquiring barrel-making skills takes years of practice, strong arms and a very good knowledge of wood. The cooper does everything by eye and experience and requires no measuring tools. Today, master coopers are highly paid craftsmen, whose barrels sell for thousands of dollars — living craftsmen continuing to prosper from a process that dates back millennia.

It is thought that Celts from Gaul (modern-day France) designed barrels, as early as 3000 BC. The Celts were skilled technicians and experts in the use of wood and metal. Historians have little to go on, but they believe these craftsmen constructed barrels, with wooden staves bound together by hoops, that closely resembled today's barrel. By the end of the second century AD, the Romans were replacing their somewhat cumbersome earthenware amphorae (pots) with lighter wooden barrels. Unlike the amphora, the barrel left no physical reminder of its presence in the Roman era. However, it does make an appearance in Roman art. Among the carved figures around Trajan's Column, an imposing stone monument in Rome, is a scene in which boats are being loaded with barrels that would have probably contained olive oil, vinegar or fish sauce.

Through the centuries that followed, the barrel enabled a growing international exchange of food. By the end of the 18th century, coopers were being engaged in the hundreds to produce barrels on an industrial scale for trade in the British Empire. At the West India Docks in London, coopers toiled throughout the day to keep up with demand for barrels. A memoir that offers historians a rare glimpse into the life of a cooper at that time described the hardships of the trade. In 1803 the author, William Hart, started working at the age of 12 for the West India Dock Company. It was a difficult time for the young apprentice. He was, he wrote, ‘very little for my age and weakly also, of a timid disposition and not one person in the place that I knew. I was away from all friends and acquaintances and very unfit for a business that required strength and energy.’

At the time, Britain's capital was the world’s largest port, alive with activity as goods arrived from all over the world. New dock facilities were being built on an unprecedented scale. The West India Docks were completed in 1802. In 1805, the London Docks opened, followed by the East India Docks in 1806. These were the equivalent of the vast container terminals seen today at ports such as Singapore, Rotterdam, Hamburg and Los Angeles, where steel shipping containers are stacked up in their thousands.

Unlike shipping containers — most of which are now manufactured in China — barrels were constructed on site. Each had to be made by hand and, when full of liquid, required constant monitoring and regular tightening to prevent leaks. As an adult, Hart was responsible for making, maintaining and monitoring a huge number of such barrels; he recalls a year in which 12,000 were under his charge. Hart's trade played an essential role in the development of food transportation, helping change society's tastes as new and exotic foodstuffs were shipped across the globe.
